title: The myth of multitasking
summary_es: Por qué hacer varias cosas a la vez es una ilusión. Colocaciones, verbos frasales y expresiones idiomáticas.
text: Few ideas about the modern workplace are as widely {{1}} as the belief that some people can do several things at once. In fact, decades of research {{2}} to the opposite conclusion. What looks like multitasking is really rapid switching between tasks, and every switch {{3}} a cost: a brief period in which the brain has to reorient itself. These moments are individually trivial, but over a working day they {{4}} up to a considerable loss. More worrying still, people who consider themselves skilled multitaskers tend to perform worst of all in laboratory tests, perhaps because they have grown {{5}} to constant interruption and no longer notice its effects. None of this means we should {{6}} to an impossible ideal of perfect concentration. Rather, psychologists suggest setting {{7}} blocks of time for demanding work and treating email as something to be dealt with in batches. The advice is hardly revolutionary, yet remarkably few organisations have taken it {{8}} board.

gaps.explanation_es: Las creencias y opiniones se «sostienen»: a widely held belief / view.
«Point to a conclusion» = apuntar a una conclusión. «Indicate» no lleva to, y «aim» va con at.
«Carry a cost / a risk / a penalty» = llevar aparejado un coste. Es la colocación para consecuencias.
«Add up to» = sumar en total, acabar siendo. Con «come» sería sin up: come to.
«Grow accustomed to» = acostumbrarse a. «Familiar» va con with.
El único que va con to + nombre: «aspire to an ideal». Los otros tres llevan complemento directo.
«Set aside time / money» = reservar. «Set apart» es distinguir y «set down», poner por escrito.
«Take something on board» = aceptar una idea o un consejo y actuar en consecuencia.
